slides.title: How can a model solve an unfamiliar task?
slides.notes:
About one minute. The goal is reliable multi-step work, not just plausible text.

The crafting game gives a clear success check. The pickaxe is a simplified illustration.

RLMs allow helper calls, but the recent crafting tests isolate one model using tools. Do not claim a demonstrated benefit from recursion.

slides.title: We tried learning from success and failure.
slides.notes:
RL is not a total failure. Answer-or-refuse tests improved from 10 to 18 successful pairs out of 64, but extra supervised training reached 19.

Planner training changed 53 to 56 correct out of 128; the gain was uncertain.

Successful crafting attempts contained rejected actions. This motivates better credit, but does not prove the cause.

slides.title: Two recent findings suggest a useful division of work.
slides.notes:
Teaching: 5 versus 15, then 3 versus 10 successes out of 32 in two training repeats. Both teachers demonstrate lookups.

Code assistance: 6 to 12, 8 to 10, 9 to 14, and 9 to 13, each out of 16.

Code uses already observed recipes, not hidden answers. Same game and related goals; no broad transfer claim.

slides.title: Can better tools make learning easier?
slides.notes:
The queued comparison crosses teaching method with code assistance on additional goals and recipe settings. It uses existing trained models.

Later RL and recursive-helper studies are proposals, not results.

Invite suggestions for another task with dependent steps and an objective success check. The candidate contribution is when this division of work helps.
